ideas.title: Lock & Current
ideas.concept: A canal-boat racing game where the locks along the river are real rotating gate discs players must physically open or close to help themselves and block their rivals. A turn feels like rolling to move your boat, deciding whether to leave a lock open (helping everyone) or slam it shut behind you, and gambling on a blind draw to fill your cargo hold.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'rotating lock gate canal boat routing board game' and 'canal lock gate board game tabletop BGG': existing canal-themed games (The Narrowboat Game, Canal Boat Race, Argy Bargey, Canal Mania, Canalis) treat locks as move-cost spaces or tile-network junctions resolved abstractly (pay a resource, place a tile) rather than as a physical two-position rotating component that any player can toggle to change the board state for everyone else. No result described a printed rotating gate disc with open/closed detents as the lock mechanism itself. The specific mechanic here — a shared physical gate that stays in whatever state the last player left it, creating a real blocking/griefing decision every turn — was not found in any of the above.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the canal board flat; each of the 4 players takes a boat token and places it on the marked Start segment; set all 6 lock-gate discs to the OPEN position; fill the draw tray with all 16 cargo chips and close its lid. Players take turns clockwise. On your turn: (1) roll the d4 and move your boat that many segments forward along the single looping canal path, stopping immediately if you would move through a lock station currently set to CLOSED (you stop on the segment just before it instead of your full roll); (2) if you moved through or landed on a segment marked with a cargo icon, draw one cargo chip blind from the tray's draw slot without looking and keep it visible in front of you; (3) if you landed exactly on a lock station, you must rotate its gate disc 90 degrees to either OPEN or CLOSED, your choice — this is the state all players will find it in on their next turn; (4) if you are carrying a cargo chip and land exactly on the matching-colored port segment, discard that chip and score 1 point. Turn passes left. The game ends the instant a player delivers their 3rd cargo chip (they win immediately) or the draw tray is emptied of chips (whoever has scored the most points wins; ties broken by whoever is furthest along the path).
ideas.components: 1x canal board, 300x300x5mm flat PLA, printed path with 40 segments and 6 lock stations and 4 colored ports; 4x boat tokens, 20x10x4mm flat hull shapes, one per player color (red/blue/green/yellow) PLA; 6x lock-gate discs, 20mm diameter x4mm thick PLA grey, each mounted on an integrated board pivot and rotatable between two detent stops; 16x cargo chips, 15mm hex x3mm thick PLA, 4 per port color; 1x draw tray, 70x70x25mm PLA box with sliding lid and a draw slot, opaque color; 1x d4 die, 18mm edge tetrahedron PLA with engraved pips 1-4; 1x lidded storage box, 320x320x60mm two-piece PLA, to hold all components.
ideas.producibility_notes: 8 distinct part types, low risk. The only joint is the lock-gate disc, a pivot-disc-with-detents design (20mm diameter) well under the ~100mm bare-bearing risk threshold flagged in prior turns; it rotates on an integrated board post between two printed stop-nubs so its two legal states (open/closed) are physically guaranteed, not tolerance-dependent. The draw tray's sliding lid is the one tolerance to call out explicitly: lid channel should be cut 0.3mm oversized versus the lid thickness for a smooth but non-rattling slide fit. No feature falls under 1mm except decorative path engraving (1mm recess), which is cosmetic only and not load-bearing.

ideas.title: Forge Row
ideas.concept: A four-season worker-placement game where every player's forging attempt pushes a single shared Heat Gauge peg along one public track — go in too cold and your tools come out weak, let the row overheat from everyone piling in and your ore is ruined. Each turn is a tense read of the shared gauge: do you forge now while it's still in the green, or wait and risk someone else pushing it into the red first.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanics: worker placement (standard) plus a push-your-luck bust mechanic. Searched 'blacksmith forge heat gauge worker placement board game peg track' and 'shared heat gauge peg track worker placement push your luck board game forging': existing blacksmith-themed worker-placement titles (Forges of Ravenshire, Blacksmiths of Steinnheimr, Forge, Metalsmith) use standard resource-to-goods conversion tracks that are private to each player, and the closest push-your-luck-plus-forging hit (Flame & Forge, an itch.io indie title) ties its risk to a combat/damage deck, not a shared physical gauge. The specific rule change here is that the Heat Gauge is a single shared component that every player's Forge action advances collectively within the same round, turning 'when do I forge' into a public information race against everyone else's actions rather than a private dice or card risk — that exact shared-gauge structure was not found in any result.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, 4 rounds ('Seasons'). Setup: place the board; each player takes 5 worker pegs in their color, a reputation peg on space 0 of the reputation track, and 2 starting ore chips; set the shared Heat Peg to space 0 of the Heat Gauge (holes 0-9, holes 3-6 are the printed Green Zone, 7-9 are the Red Zone). Each round, players alternate placing one worker peg per turn onto any open slot (3 slots per space) on one of the 6 action spaces: Ore Pit (take 2 ore chips), Charcoal Yard (take 2 coal chips), Market (sell any 1 tool token for 2 coin chips), Guild Hall (advance your reputation peg 1 space), Rest (take back all your placed workers early, ending your placements for the round), or Forge (pay 1 ore chip + 1 coal chip to the supply, then move the shared Heat Peg forward 2 spaces: if the Heat Peg is now in the Green Zone, take 1 Tool token worth 3 points; if it is now in the Red Zone, your ore and coal are lost with no tool; if it is still below the Green Zone, you may instead bank your ore and coal unspent for next round). Once all workers are placed or all players have chosen Rest, the round ends: reset the Heat Peg to 0 and return all worker pegs to their owners. After 4 rounds, each player scores 3 points per Tool token, 1 point per coin chip, and 1 point per space their reputation peg has advanced. Highest total wins; ties go to whoever has more unused ore+coal chips.
ideas.components: 1x board, 250x200x5mm PLA, printed with 6 action spaces (3 worker slots each), a 10-hole Heat Gauge track, and an 8-hole Reputation track; 20x worker pegs, 8mm diameter x20mm tall cylinders, 5 per player in 4 colors; 1x Heat Peg, 6mm diameter x15mm tall, red/black PLA, distinct from worker pegs; 4x Reputation pegs, 4mm diameter x10mm tall, matching player colors; 12x ore chips, 12mm hex x3mm, brown PLA; 12x coal chips, 12mm hex x3mm, black PLA; 16x coin chips, 12mm diameter disc x2mm, gold PLA; 12x tool tokens, 14mm diamond x3mm, silver PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 8 part types, all peg-in-hole joints only (no rotating or hinged parts). Worker peg diameter 8mm into 8.4mm sockets (0.4mm clearance) is a proven, low-risk fit; Heat Peg and Reputation pegs use the same 4-4.4mm peg-in-hole standard. No feature under 1mm except cosmetic icon engravings on tokens (0.3mm recess, non-functional). The Heat Gauge's failure/success behavior is fully deterministic from printed zone boundaries and peg position — there is no physical give, friction, or balance dependency, so the 'push-your-luck' feel comes entirely from player decisions, not from any unvalidated physical mechanism.

ideas.title: Compass Trick
ideas.concept: A trick-taking game where trump isn't chosen by anyone — after every trick, a shared compass needle automatically swings to point at the suit of the single highest-numbered tile that was just played, and that becomes trump for the next trick. A turn feels like watching the needle after your trick and instantly recalculating which suit you now need to hoard or dump.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: trick-taking with a trump suit. Searched 'trump suit rotating compass dial trick-taking board game' and 'Marjapussi card game changing trump rules': the closest precedent for a mid-hand-changing trump is the traditional Finnish game Marjapussi, where trump changes when a player chooses to declare a king-queen 'marriage' of a suit — a player-initiated, opt-in event. This design's rule change is that the trump-suit change is fully deterministic and mandatory, driven by a physical shared dial rather than a player declaration: the suit of the single highest tile played in the just-finished trick becomes trump next, with no player choice involved, and no result found described a physical rotating trump indicator with this deterministic post-trick trigger.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players (rules below assume 4; scale hand size to floor(40/players)). Setup: mix the 40 suit tiles face down and deal 10 to each of 4 players, forming a hand held upright in each player's hand rack out of others' view. Place the Compass base in the center with the needle disc mounted on its peg. Roll the d4 once to set the needle to a starting suit (Coin=1, Cup=2, Sword=3, Star=4) by rotating it to that detent. Choose a starting player. Play proceeds trick by trick: the leader plays any tile from their hand face up in front of them; each other player in turn order must play a tile of the same suit if they hold one, otherwise any tile. A trick is won by the highest tile of the led suit, unless one or more Compass-suit (trump) tiles were played, in which case the highest trump tile wins regardless of what was led. The trick winner takes all played tiles into their trick tray and leads the next trick. After the trick is resolved and before the next one begins, rotate the Compass needle to point at the suit of whichever single tile in that trick had the highest printed number (regardless of who played it or who won) — this is the new trump suit for the next trick. Continue until all 10 tricks are played. Score 1 point per tile in each trick you won. Play 3 hands total (re-shuffle and re-deal, alternating starting player); sum points across all 3 hands. Highest total wins; ties share the win.
ideas.components: 40x suit tiles, 40x25x3mm rectangular PLA, cream/white, engraved with 1 of 4 suit icons (coin, cup, sword, star) and a number 1-10; 1x compass base, 100x100x8mm circular PLA disc, grey, with a central 6mm diameter x10mm tall peg and 4 suit icons printed at N/E/S/W; 1x compass needle, 60mm long arrow-shaped disc x3mm thick, red PLA, with a 6.4mm center hole and 4 underside detent dimples; 4x trick trays, 90x60x15mm open PLA trays, one per player color; 4x hand racks, 150x20x20mm PLA troughs with a 3mm-wide top slot to hold tiles upright and hidden, one per player color; 1x d4 die (shared design with Idea 1's die), 18mm edge tetrahedron PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 part types. The compass needle is a pivot-disc-with-detents joint at only 60mm span (well under the ~100mm bare-bearing risk threshold) rotating on an integrated base peg with 4 printed detent stops — fully deterministic 4-position mechanism, not friction-dependent. Suit tiles and hand racks are simple flat/slot geometry with no joints; the hand-rack slot (3mm wide) should be printed 0.4mm oversized versus the 3mm tile thickness for tiles to stand and slide freely without binding. No feature under 1mm except icon engraving (0.3mm, cosmetic only).

ideas.title: Terrace Stack
ideas.concept: Players build up rice-terrace hillside fields by stacking colored rings onto fixed pegs, then declare a crop and harvest whichever ring currently sits on top of a matching-color stack for points based on how high it was buried. A turn is either a blind risk — placing an unseen ring onto a growing stack — or a calculated grab, calling your crop and cashing in the top ring before someone else buries it deeper.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'wedge tile stacking rice terrace board game': the nearest hits (Terrace, a 3D level-based abstract strategy game from the 1970s; Stakz, a match-and-stack family game; NMBR 9, a flat overlapping-number stacking puzzle) all use open unconstrained stacking or flat overlap, not fixed vertical pegs that mechanically cap and order each stack. This design's stacks are individually pegged (one peg per hex field, capped at 4 rings) so height and stacking order are structurally guaranteed rather than balance-dependent, and scoring is tied to a blind-draw-then-declare harvesting decision rather than pure spatial puzzle-solving — that specific combination was not found in any result.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the hex board in the center; fill the draw tray with all 76 terrace rings (19 each of green/yellow/brown/grey) and close its lid; each player takes a personal score pegboard and places their score peg at 0. On your turn, choose one: (A) Draw a ring blind from the tray's draw slot without looking, then place it on top of any hex field's peg that currently holds fewer than 4 rings (you choose which field, but not which ring you drew); or (B) Harvest: declare aloud a crop color, then look at every hex field on the board and remove the topmost ring from any ONE field where the top ring matches your declared color; score points equal to that ring's position in the stack (1st ring placed on that peg = 1 point, 2nd = 2 points, 3rd = 3 points, 4th = 4 points) by moving your score peg forward that many spaces; discard the harvested ring to the box (it is out of play). You may only harvest a field where the top ring visibly matches your call — if no field qualifies, you may not harvest this turn and must draw instead. The game ends immediately when the draw tray is empty and no legal harvest is available to the active player. Highest score wins; ties share the win.
ideas.components: 1x hex board, 250mm diameter x8mm thick PLA, green/brown, with 19 hexagonal fields (35mm point-to-point) each bearing an integrated vertical peg 4mm diameter x30mm tall; 76x terrace rings, annular rings 25mm outer diameter x4.6mm inner hole x6mm tall, 19 each in green/yellow/brown/grey PLA; 4x personal score pegboards, 100x20x5mm PLA strips with 10 holes and a score peg, one per player color; 1x draw tray, 90x90x30mm PLA box with sliding lid and draw slot (shared design family with Idea 1's tray, scaled up).
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 part types, minimal risk. The ring-on-peg stacking is deterministic by construction, not a balance-dependent mechanic: each peg is 30mm tall and each ring is 6mm tall, so a maximum 4-ring stack (24mm) always leaves clearance and physically cannot topple or lean past its peg — there is no player-facing tolerance that could fail, unlike a freestanding block-stacking game. The one dimension to hold precisely is the ring inner hole at 4.6mm against the 4mm peg (0.3mm radial clearance per side) for rings to slide on freely without wobbling loose. No feature under 1mm except cosmetic hex-field engraving.

ideas.title: Fox & Lantern
ideas.concept: A two-player sowing game built on classic Kalah mancala rules, with one new twist: four pits on the board hold a fixed Lantern marker, and any time your last sown seed lands in a lantern pit, you immediately reverse direction and keep sowing your remaining seeds the other way around the board. A turn is the familiar mancala scoop-and-drop rhythm, punctuated by a sudden direction flip that can turn a losing sow into a capture.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: Kalah-rules Mancala sowing and capture. Searched 'directional redirect tokens mancala sowing game variant': existing documented sowing variants (reverse sowing/Reaping, partisan sowing, two-dimensional sowing, stacking variants like Rondell and Martian Mancala) change who may sow in which direction or add stacking, but none of the surveyed variants use a fixed in-board marker that triggers a mid-sow direction reversal the instant a seed lands on it. The specific rule change here — a persistent Lantern token in 4 of the 12 pits that flips sowing direction whenever the currently-sown seed lands there, potentially flipping multiple times in one turn — was not found in the surveyed mancala variant literature.
ideas.rules: 2 players. Setup: place the board with 6 pits per side plus 2 end stores. Before adding seeds, place 1 Lantern token into each of 4 marked pits (2 on each side, at the positions marked with a lantern icon on the board) — Lantern tokens stay in their pit for the entire game and are never picked up or sown. Then place 4 seed tokens into every pit (including the pits that already contain a Lantern). Players sit on opposite sides; each owns the 6 pits on their side and the store to their right. On your turn, choose one of your own non-empty pits, pick up all seed tokens in it (leave any Lantern token behind), and sow them one at a time into each following pit going counter-clockwise, including your own store but skipping your opponent's store. If the seed you are sowing is the one that lands in a pit containing a Lantern token, immediately reverse your sowing direction to clockwise for all remaining seeds in that same turn (if a later seed in the same turn lands on another Lantern pit, reverse again). Standard capture rule: if your very last sown seed lands in a pit on your own side that was empty before that seed, capture that seed plus all seeds in the directly opposite pit, moving them all to your store. The game ends when one player's 6 pits are all empty on their turn; the other player moves all remaining seeds on their side into their own store. The player with more seeds in their store wins; equal stores is a tie.
ideas.components: 1x board, 300x120x15mm PLA wood-look tan, with 12 pits (30mm diameter x10mm deep, 2 rows of 6) and 2 end stores (50x40x12mm oval recesses); 48x seed tokens, faceted acorn shapes 10mm tall, brown PLA; 4x lantern tokens, lantern-shaped 14mm tall x12mm diameter base, translucent-yellow PLA, placed in 4 marked pits at setup.
ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types, the simplest build in this batch: zero joints of any kind, every piece is a loose token resting in an open pit. No rotating, hinged, or press-fit parts anywhere. The only geometric requirement is that pits (30mm diameter) comfortably hold up to roughly 12-14 loose tokens (10mm each) without overflow, which is generously sized. No feature under 1mm.

ideas.title: Cargo Hold
ideas.concept: A dice-drafting cargo game where the shape of the freight you get is decided by which die you draft from a shared dock roll, and then you must physically pack it into your own ship's grid before the next round. A turn feels like Tetris under time pressure: grab the best-shaped die before your rivals do, then find the one spot on your hold where that piece still fits.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanics: dice drafting (as in The Great Harbor) and polyomino grid-packing (as in Patchwork and Barenpark). Searched 'dice drafting shipping cargo board game engraved chips harbor' and 'cargo ship hold grid polyomino packing dice draft board game': The Great Harbor uses dice drafting purely for worker-placement action resolution with no spatial packing; Patchwork/Isle of Cats/Barenpark use fixed tile sets drawn from a bag or timing track, not dice; ShipShape and Curious Cargo use bidding or facility-building rather than dice-determined tile shapes. This design's specific combination — a shared dice roll each round determines which polyomino shape each drafted die awards, immediately packed onto a personal fixed-size grid and scored by completed rows/columns rather than raw area or an income track — was not found as a single existing product in these results.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, 6 rounds. Setup: each player takes a 6x6 Ship Hold board. Place the 5 Dock Dice in the center. At the start of each round, roll all 5 Dock Dice together. In turn order (rotating each round), each player picks one remaining die from the dock, notes its shape icon (1x1, 1x2, 1x3, 2x2, or L-tromino), and takes one matching cargo tile of their choice of color from the general supply. They must then immediately place that tile flat on their own Ship Hold grid, fully within the 6x6 boundary and not overlapping any tile already placed; if it cannot legally be placed anywhere, it is discarded unplaced and that player scores nothing for it. Once all 5 dice are drafted (in a 2-3 player game, re-roll and continue drafting from the remaining/reset dice until every player has drafted once per round), the round ends and all dice return to the dock for the next round's roll. After 6 rounds, each player scores 1 point per grid cell covered by a tile, plus 3 bonus points for each fully covered row or column, minus 1 point for each cell still empty. Highest total score wins; ties share the win.

This is a deterministic, tolerance-free design — tile placement success or failure is a pure logic/fit question decided by the player, not by any physical press-fit, rotation, or balance mechanism. The only dimension to hold is the grid ridge height (1mm) staying low enough that tiles still sit flush and don't rock, which is a cosmetic/functional detail with generous tolerance.

ideas.title: Glyph Cipher
ideas.concept: A two-player codebreaking duel built on Mastermind-style guess-and-feedback logic, but instead of picking colored pegs from a supply, each player sets their code and their guesses by rotating four rune-symbol dials mounted directly on the board. A turn is a tactile twist-and-lock: dial in your guess, call it, and watch your opponent slot rune-shaped feedback pegs into the result strip.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: Mastermind-style code-breaking with black/white peg feedback. Searched 'rotating rune disc codebreaking deduction board game two player': the closest hits (Codebreak, Break the Code, classic Mastermind, Runes) all use either loose colored pegs placed into a peg-hole grid, face-up number tiles behind a screen, or word-guessing, with no result describing rotating symbol dials as the input method for setting or guessing a code. The specific rule/component change here is replacing discrete peg-placement (which requires a supply of many loose pegs per color) with four fixed rotating dials per board that are simply twisted to a new symbol each guess, changing the physical guessing action from 'pick up and place a piece' to 'rotate a dial' while keeping the same black/white-style feedback logic — that exact substitution was not found in the surveyed results.
ideas.rules: 2 players, played over 2 rounds (swap codemaker/codebreaker roles each round; higher combined score across both rounds wins). Each round: the Codemaker secretly rotates the 4 rune dials on their Code Board to a sequence of their choice (repeats of a symbol allowed; 6 possible rune symbols per dial), then slides the Privacy Screen into place hiding the dials from the Codebreaker. The Codebreaker rotates the 4 dials on their own Guess Strip to a guessed sequence and announces 'guess' aloud. The Codemaker checks the guess against their hidden code and places Feedback Pegs into the Guess Strip's 4-hole feedback row: one black peg for each dial that matches the hidden code in both symbol and position, one white peg (no black pegs for that match) for each dial whose symbol appears somewhere in the code but in a different position, with no peg for symbols that don't appear at all. The Codebreaker rotates the dials to a new guess and repeats. If the Codebreaker matches the code exactly within 8 guesses, they score (9 minus the number of guesses used) points; if they fail to match it within 8 guesses, the Codemaker scores 4 points for that round. Swap roles for round 2 with a new secret code. Sum each player's points across both rounds; higher total wins, a tie is a shared win.
ideas.components: 2x Code Boards, 120x60x10mm PLA dark grey, each with 4 rotating rune dials on integrated pegs and 2 slide-in grooves for a privacy screen; 2x Privacy Screens, 130x70x3mm flat PLA panels with 2 bottom tabs, opaque; 2x Guess Strips, 120x40x10mm PLA light grey, each with 4 rotating rune dials plus a 4-hole feedback peg row; 16x rune dials total (8 across the 2 Code Boards, 8 across the 2 Guess Strips), 18mm diameter x6mm thick discs with 6 engraved rune symbols around the rim, PLA; 64x feedback pegs, 4mm diameter x8mm tall, 32 black + 32 white, PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types. Rune dials are pivot-disc-with-detents joints at only 18mm diameter (well within the proven low-risk range from prior successful builds), rotating on an integrated 6mm peg with 6 printed detent stops so each dial has exactly 6 legal rest positions, fully deterministic. The Privacy Screen uses a slide-in peg-and-groove fit rather than a hinge, avoiding hinge-tolerance risk entirely: the 2 tabs (10x3mm) should be printed 0.3mm undersized versus the 3.3mm-wide grooves for a smooth slide. Feedback pegs are standard peg-in-hole (4mm peg into 4.4mm socket). No feature under 1mm except the engraved rune symbols (0.3mm recess, cosmetic).

ideas.cad_prompt: Design a complete physical tabletop board game kit as separate CAD-modelable FDM-printable PLA parts. Part 1: Code Board, quantity 2, each a flat rectangular base 120mm x 60mm x 10mm thick, with 4 integrated upright pegs 6mm diameter x 8mm tall spaced 25mm apart in a row across the top surface, and two parallel grooves 3.3mm wide x 10mm deep x 70mm long cut into the base perpendicular to the peg row, positioned 60mm apart, to accept a slide-in privacy screen, material PLA, color dark grey. Part 2: Privacy Screen, quantity 2, a flat panel 130mm x 70mm x 3mm thick, opaque, with two tabs on the bottom edge each 10mm wide x 3mm thick x 8mm tall sized 0.3mm undersized versus the Code Board's 3.3mm grooves for a smooth slide fit, material PLA, opaque dark color. Part 3: Guess Strip, quantity 2, a flat rectangular base 120mm x 40mm x 10mm thick, with 4 integrated upright pegs 6mm diameter x 8mm tall spaced 25mm apart in a row (identical peg layout to the Code Board), plus a separate row of 4 round sockets 4.4mm diameter x 4mm deep spaced 8mm apart for feedback pegs, material PLA, color light grey. Part 4: Rune Dial, quantity 16, each a disc 18mm diameter x 6mm thick with 6 distinct rune symbols engraved around the outer rim at 60-degree intervals, with a center through-hole 6.4mm diameter fitting over the 6mm pegs on Part 1 or Part 3 with 0.4mm clearance for free rotation, and 6 small 1mm-deep detent dimples on the underside at 60-degree intervals matching 6 raised 1mm nubs printed around each peg's base so the dial rests at exactly 6 positions, material PLA, natural/tan color with dark engraving. Part 5: Feedback Peg, quantity 64 (32 black, 32 white), each a cylinder 4mm diameter x 8mm tall, material PLA. All parts are separate components; rotating dials use a simple peg-and-disc assembly with printed detents, and the privacy screen uses a slide-in tab-and-groove fit, with no glue required anywhere.

ideas.title: Caravan Ledger
ideas.concept: A pick-up-and-deliver trading game where every player's progress is tracked on one shared public ledger strip instead of hidden cards, so everyone always knows exactly how close their rivals are to winning. A turn is equal parts route-planning and open psychological pressure: move your caravan, grab or deliver goods in full view, and watch the shared ledger tick forward for whoever's closing in fastest.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: pick-up-and-deliver route trading. Searched 'pickup and deliver trade route board game engraved ledger tiles instead of cards': surveyed pick-up-and-deliver games (Express Route, Cargo Empire, Xia-style deliveries) track delivery progress and goods privately via player hands, personal boards, or money tracks that rivals can't easily read at a glance. This design's rule change is making delivery progress fully public on one shared physical ledger track (rather than a private score pad or hand of delivery cards) and adding a Toll rule where landing on another player's caravan lets you take one of their visibly-held goods chips directly (no die roll needed, since the goods are always visible) — that specific combination of a shared public progress track plus a guaranteed-by-visibility steal rule was not found in the surveyed results.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. Setup: place the board showing 10 city nodes connected by paths, each city marked with 1-2 goods icons it produces and a 'wants' icon on its far face; each player places their caravan peg on a different starting city and their ledger peg on space 0 of the shared 30-space Ledger Track; fill the general supply with the 48 goods chips (12 each of spice/silk/salt/tea). On your turn, move your caravan peg up to 3 path-segments total (each segment crossed costs 1 of your 3 movement). After moving, resolve any one of the following if applicable: (a) if you are at a city, you may take 1 goods chip matching that city's produced icon from the general supply, keeping it visibly stacked in front of you (no limit to how many you may hold); (b) if you are at a city whose 'wants' icon matches a goods chip you are holding, you may deliver it: return the chip to the supply and advance your ledger peg forward on the shared track by the number printed on the path segment(s) you most recently crossed to arrive there (1-4 per segment, longer routes are worth more); (c) if your caravan lands on the same city node as another player's caravan, you may take 1 goods chip of your choice from that player's visible stock instead of taking one from the city (a 'Toll'). The game ends immediately when any player's ledger peg reaches space 30; that player wins outright.
ideas.components: 1x board, 250x250x6mm PLA tan, 10 city node recesses connected by printed paths with distance values, plus a 30-hole shared Ledger Track along one edge; 4x caravan pegs, camel-silhouette tokens 20mm tall x8mm base, 4 colors; 4x ledger pegs, 4mm diameter x10mm tall, matching colors; 48x goods chips, 12mm hex x3mm, 4 types x12 each (spice purple, silk red, salt white, tea green).
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 part types, all simple peg-in-hole or loose-resting pieces, zero rotating or hinged joints. Caravan pegs rest loosely in shallow 12mm city-node recesses (not a tight socket, so no tolerance risk); ledger pegs use the same 4mm peg into 4.4mm hole standard as other ideas in this batch. No feature under 1mm except path distance-value engravings (cosmetic).

ideas.title: Sunstone Circle
ideas.concept: The traditional Kalah mancala ruleset, restyled as a celestial stone-circle altar: one side of the board is etched with a sunburst rim, the other with a crescent-moon rim, and the sown seeds are small faceted star-shaped tokens captured into sun-disc and moon-crescent store bowls. A turn plays exactly like classic mancala, but the table presence is an ancient astronomical relic rather than a plain wooden board.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: traditional Kalah-rules Mancala (public domain folk game, rules unchanged from standard play). Searched 'celestial sun moon themed mancala board game': results returned unrelated sun/moon-themed games (Sun, Moon, & Stars deduction game; Sun & Moon Stonehenge expansion; Madoshi Priests of the Sun and Moon) and general mancala listings, but no existing product combining standard Kalah mancala with a sun/moon celestial stone-circle art and component styling. This is styling-only: no rule differs from standard Kalah play.
ideas.rules: 2 players, standard Kalah rules. Setup: each of the 12 pits (6 per side) gets 4 seed tokens; each player owns the 6 pits nearest them and the store to their right (sun-disc bowl for one player, moon-crescent bowl for the other, assigned by seating, purely cosmetic). On your turn, pick up all seeds from one of your own non-empty pits and sow them one at a time counter-clockwise into each following pit, including your own store but skipping your opponent's store. If your last sown seed lands in your own previously-empty pit, capture that seed plus all seeds in the directly opposite pit into your store. If your last sown seed lands in your own store, take another turn. The game ends when one player's side is completely empty on their turn; the other player sweeps all remaining seeds on their side into their own store. Most seeds in your store wins; equal is a tie.
ideas.components: 1x board, 300x120x15mm PLA cream/gold marbled, 12 pits (30mm diameter x10mm deep) with an engraved sunburst rim on one long side and an engraved crescent-moon rim on the other, plus 2 store-bowl recesses (50x40x12mm) at the ends, one engraved with a sunburst, one with a crescent moon; 48x seed tokens, 5-pointed star-bead shape 10mm point-to-point, gold/cream PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 2 part types, the lowest-risk build in the entire batch: zero joints, all seeds are loose tokens resting in open pit recesses, identical structurally to Fox & Lantern's board minus the lantern markers. No feature under 1mm except the decorative sunburst/crescent rim engravings (0.5mm recess, cosmetic only).

All parts are loose, unconnected components with no joints; all tokens simply rest inside the board's pit and store recesses.

ideas.title: Frost Nine
ideas.concept: The classic Nine Men's Morris ruleset, restyled as a battle fought across a cracked frozen lake: the board's mill lines are engraved as ice fractures, and the two sides play as faceted crystal pegs — clear Frost Shards versus dark blue Deepwater gems. A turn plays exactly like traditional Nine Men's Morris, but the physical piece feels like planting gemstones into a frozen surface rather than moving plain checkers.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: traditional Nine Men's Morris (ancient public-domain folk game dating to at least the Roman Empire; rules unchanged from standard play, including the standard flying-rule endgame variant). Searched 'ice glacier themed nine men's morris board game': results returned generic and custom/Etsy Nine Men's Morris boards with no ice/glacier theme identified, and no existing shipped product combining Nine Men's Morris with a frozen-lake art direction and faceted crystal-peg components. This is styling-only: no rule differs from standard Nine Men's Morris play.
ideas.rules: 2 players, standard Nine Men's Morris rules. Setup: place the board showing 3 concentric squares connected by 4 midpoint lines, forming 24 intersection points; each player takes 9 pieces (9 Frost Shard for one player, 9 Deepwater for the other). Phase 1 (placing): players alternate placing one piece on any empty point; whenever a player completes a straight line of 3 of their own pieces along a printed line ('a mill'), they immediately remove one opponent piece from the board (not from a currently-formed opposing mill unless no other option exists). Phase 2 (moving): once all 18 pieces are placed, players alternate sliding one of their own pieces along a printed line to an adjacent empty point, forming mills the same way to capture opponent pieces (a piece may be broken and re-formed into a mill repeatedly for repeated captures across turns). Flying rule: once a player is reduced to exactly 3 pieces, that player may move any of their pieces to any empty point on the board (not just adjacent ones) for the rest of the game. A player loses when reduced to 2 pieces or when they cannot legally move on their turn.
ideas.components: 1x board, 300x300x8mm PLA white/blue marbled, printed with 3 concentric square outlines (outer 260mm, middle 170mm, inner 80mm) connected by 4 midpoint lines, all engraved 0.5mm deep as ice-crack texture, with 24 intersection sockets (4mm diameter x5mm deep); 18x crystal pegs, 9 white 'Frost Shard' and 9 blue 'Deepwater', each a faceted gem-cut peg with a 4mm diameter x3mm peg base and a 10mm tall hexagonal-faceted crystal top.
ideas.producibility_notes: 2 part types, extremely low risk: pure peg-in-hole placement (4mm peg into 4.4mm socket, 0.4mm clearance), no rotating or hinged parts, no balance dependency. No feature under 1mm except the ice-crack line engraving (0.5mm, cosmetic only).
ideas.prompt: Product photo of an icy-themed abstract strategy board game: a square white-and-blue marbled board with three nested square outlines connected by cross lines, all etched like cracks in frozen ice, small faceted crystal pegs in clear/white and deep blue standing at intersection points, cold blue-white lighting, dramatic winter color palette, matching square product box behind showing a frozen lake illustration.
ideas.cad_prompt: Design a complete physical tabletop board game kit as separate CAD-modelable FDM-printable PLA parts. Part 1: Frost Board, quantity 1, a flat square slab 300mm x 300mm x 8mm thick, top surface engraved with 3 concentric square line outlines (outer square 260mm x 260mm, middle square 170mm x 170mm, inner square 80mm x 80mm, all centered) connected by 4 straight lines running from the midpoint of each outer square edge inward to the corresponding middle and inner square edge midpoints, all lines engraved 0.5mm deep with an irregular jagged ice-crack texture, and 24 round sockets 4.4mm diameter x 5mm deep at every corner and midpoint intersection along these lines (8 sockets per square x 3 squares), material PLA, color white/blue marbled. Part 2: Crystal Peg, quantity 18 (9 white, 9 blue), each with a cylindrical base peg 4mm diameter x 3mm tall and a faceted hexagonal-prism crystal top 10mm tall x 8mm across the flats, tapering slightly to a point at the very top, sized so the base peg fits the Frost Board's 4.4mm sockets with 0.4mm clearance, material PLA, 9 in white/clear color and 9 in dark blue color. All parts are separate loose components using simple peg-in-hole placement with no glue, hinge, or press-fit required.

cad_build_picks.reason: Lock & Current uses only proven joint types (a small pivot-disc-with-detents lock gate at 20mm diameter, well below the ~100mm bare-bearing risk line, plus simple slide-fit tray and flat tokens), giving high confidence of a clean zero-intervention build that visibly matches the pitched canal-routing concept.

Fox & Lantern has zero joints of any kind (board + loose seed tokens + loose lantern tokens only), making it the single lowest-risk build in the batch while still carrying a genuinely verified rule-level twist on Kalah mancala, so it should build clean and score well on both producibility and fidelity.

Cargo Hold is entirely flat, loose-resting geometry (grid boards, cube dice, flat polyomino tiles) with no press-fits, hinges, or rotating parts anywhere, so build failure risk is minimal, and its dice-shape-to-grid-packing combination is confirmed distinct from the nearest named comparables (Great Harbor, Patchwork, ShipShape).
